files.lesson.md: --- order: 53 unit: boxplots10 node: AC9M10ST02 n2 uses: [AC9M10ST02 n1] assumes: [AC9M10ST02 n1] connection: bus-lateness title: Boxplots summary: "A boxplot draws the five numbers as one picture: the box is the middle half, the bar is the median, and the whiskers reach the lowest and highest values that aren't outliers." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "You catch Route 1 to school, and it's late sometimes. How late is it on a normal day?" app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8446 url: http://127.0.0.1:8446/index.html readySelector: "#board" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: data.yml#pic, caption: "Route 1: lowest 0, lower quartile 2, median 4, upper quartile 6, highest 15. The 15 is an outlier, so the upper whisker stops at 8." } --- The Route 1 bus app gives the minutes the bus was late on each of the last 11 school days: 0, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 8 and 15 (made up for the task). One bad day looks bad, but you want to know about the normal days. A boxplot shows the middle half of the days as a box, with a bar at the median. Have a guess where the box would start and end, and we'll check. ## Predict: where the box goes ```step stage: predict insight: "Choosing where the box starts and ends shows who treats the box as the whole data set and who sees it as the middle half." check: type: predict q: "A boxplot's box covers the middle half of the days. Where would the box start and end for Route 1?" options: - "From 0 to 15, all the days" - "From 1 to 8" - "From 2 to 6" - "From 3 to 5" actual: "From 2 to 6. The lower quartile is 2 and the upper quartile is 6, so half the days fall in the box. The median bar sits at 4." ``` ## Run: take out the very late day ```step stage: run insight: "The cross marks a value so far from the box that it counts as an outlier. Bring the value back towards the rest and it joins the whisker." try: { playground: board, starter: "data.yml#run", height: 600 } check: { type: board, text: "The 15 shows as a cross, not part of the whisker. Change the 15 to 9 in the Values box and press Use these values. What happens to the cross?", when: "q_out = 0 and h = 9", explain: "With a 9 instead of the 15 there is no cross: 9 is inside the fence, which is 6 + 1.5 × 4 = 12, so the whisker reaches it." } ``` The box runs from the lower quartile to the upper quartile, the thick bar is the median, and the whiskers reach the lowest and highest values that aren't outliers. A cross marks an outlier. ## Investigate: reading and drawing a boxplot ```step stage: investigate insight: "The box is the middle half of the data and its length is the interquartile range; the whiskers reach the furthest values inside the fences; a value beyond a fence is an outlier. The width of the box says how spread out the middle half is, not how many values there are." tasks: - hint: ["Find the IQR first, then 1.5 times it.", "Upper fence = upper quartile + 1.5 × IQR."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A bus's lateness has five numbers 1, 3, 4, 8 and 20 (minutes, made up). What is the upper fence, and is 20 an outlier?" steps: - ["$8 - 3 = 5$", "the interquartile range, upper quartile take away lower quartile"] - ["$1.5 \\times 5 = 7.5$", "the distance allowed beyond the box"] - ["$8 + 7.5 = 15.5$", "the upper fence"] - ["$20 > 15.5$, so 20 is an outlier", "it is beyond the fence"] answer: "15.5" answerLabel: "Upper fence (minutes)" tolerance: 0.01 feedback: - ["12.5", "That is the upper quartile plus the IQR. The rule is 1.5 times the IQR."] - ["20", "That is the highest value. The fence is the upper quartile plus 1.5 times the IQR."] criteria: - "I found the interquartile range." - "I found 1.5 times the IQR and added it to the upper quartile." - "I compared the highest value with the fence." explain: "IQR = 8 − 3 = 5, and 1.5 × 5 = 7.5, so the upper fence is 8 + 7.5 = 15.5. The 20 is beyond it, so it is an outlier." - hint: ["The box is the middle half of the data.", "Which two of the five numbers mark the middle half?"] check: type: question q: "A boxplot's five numbers are 2, 5, 8, 13 and 21. Which two numbers are the ends of the box?" options: - "5 and 13" - "2 and 21" - "5 and 8" - "8 and 13" answer: 0 feedback: - null - "Those are the lowest and highest values, the ends of the whiskers (if there are no outliers)." - "The 8 is the median, the bar inside the box. The box runs from 5 to 13." - "The 8 is the median. The box also goes down to the lower quartile, 5." explain: "The box runs from the lower quartile (5) to the upper quartile (13), with the median bar at 8. The whiskers reach to 2 and 21 if neither is an outlier." smaller: check: type: question q: "The box starts at the lower quartile. Where does it end?" options: - "At the upper quartile" - "At the highest value" - "At the median" answer: 0 feedback: - null - "The highest value is the end of the upper whisker, outside the box." - "The median is the bar inside the box." explain: "The box covers the middle half, from the lower quartile to the upper quartile." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#dev" text: "Dev compares two bus routes' boxplots. Click the line where the reading goes wrong." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: box-width-is-count explain: "Line 3: the width of a box is how far apart the quartiles are, so it shows the spread of the middle half. Each box holds half of that route's days, whatever its width." - check: type: question q: "The median bar in a boxplot sits close to the left end of the box (the quartiles are 3 and 12 and the median is 5). What does this tell you?" options: - "The values between 3 and 5 are bunched closer together than the values between 5 and 12" - "More days are on the left than on the right" - "The data has no outliers" - "The mean equals the median" answer: 0 feedback: - null - "A quarter of the days is on each side of the median bar, whatever its position." - "Outliers show as crosses outside the whiskers, not through the median's position." - "A median near one end hints that the mean and median differ, not that they match." explain: "A quarter of the days lie on each side of the median. If the median is near the left end, that quarter is squeezed into a small range, while the other quarter is spread out more." ``` ### Reading the fences ```worked 0, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 8, 15 :: Route 1's eleven days, in order. \text{lowest } 0,\ Q_1 = 2,\ \text{median } 4,\ Q_3 = 6,\ \text{highest } 15 :: The five numbers. 6 - 2 = 4 :: The box's length, the interquartile range. 6 + 1.5 \times 4 = 12 :: The upper fence: values beyond it are outliers. 15 > 12 :: So 15 is an outlier. It is drawn as a cross. \text{upper whisker to } 8 :: The whisker stops at the highest value inside the fence. ``` Now try one on paper: a bus's lateness has five numbers 1, 3, 4, 8 and 20 minutes. Work out the upper fence and decide whether the 20 is an outlier. ### Box ends ### Find the mistake Route 2's lateness on the same 11 days (made up) is 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 6 and 7, so its quartiles are 4 and 6. ### The median bar ## Modify: change the data ```step stage: modify insight: "Moving a value or flattening the data shows when a whisker grows to meet a value, and what happens when every value is the same." try: { playground: board, starter: "data.yml#modify", height: 600 } tasks: - check: { type: board, text: "Change the 15 to 11 in the Values box and press Use these values. Does the cross stay?", when: "q_out = 0 and h = 11", explain: "No: the upper fence is still 6 + 1.5 × 4 = 12, and 11 is inside it, so the whisker reaches 11. The cross is gone." } - hint: ["Every value is 5, so the lowest, the quartiles, the median and the highest are all 5.", "5 − 5."] check: { type: number, q: "Edge case: type 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5 into the Values box. What is the interquartile range?", answer: 0, tolerance: 0, explain: "Every number in the five-number summary is 5, so the box has no length. The boxplot is a single bar." } - hint: ["A value exactly on the fence isn't beyond it.", "The upper fence is 12."] check: type: question q: "Edge case: Route 1 has a day that is exactly 12 minutes late. The upper fence is 12. Is that day an outlier?" options: - "No: an outlier is beyond the fence, and 12 is on it" - "Yes: 12 is far above the median" - "Yes: every value on a fence is an outlier" - "No: no value is ever an outlier" answer: 0 feedback: - null - "The rule is about the fence, not about how far above the median it is." - "The rule is 'beyond the fence', so a value on the fence stays in the whisker." - "Values beyond the fences are outliers." explain: "The rule says a value is an outlier when it is more than 1.5 × IQR beyond the box. At exactly 12 it is not more than that, so the whisker reaches 12." ``` ### A smaller late day ### All the same ### Exactly on the fence ## Practise: reading and fences ```step stage: practise insight: "Reading the box's length, the fence and the outlier decision from five numbers, with a review of the lower quartile." tasks: - hint: ["Upper quartile take away lower quartile.", "31 is the highest value, not the upper quartile."] check: { type: number, q: "A boxplot's five numbers are 4, 9, 13, 20 and 31. What is the interquartile range?", answer: 11, tolerance: 0, explain: "The quartiles are 9 and 20, so the IQR is 20 − 9 = 11." } - hint: ["1.5 × the IQR, added to the upper quartile.", "1.5 × 11 = 16.5."] check: { type: number, q: "For those five numbers (4, 9, 13, 20, 31), what is the upper fence?", answer: 36.5, tolerance: 0.01, explain: "20 + 1.5 × 11 = 20 + 16.5 = 36.5. The highest value, 31, is inside it, so it isn't an outlier." } - hint: ["Nine values: leave the median out of both halves.", "The lower half is the first four values."] check: { type: number, q: "Review: nine values in order are 3, 5, 8, 10, 12, 14, 17, 19 and 25. What is the lower quartile?", answer: 6.5, tolerance: 0.01, explain: "The median is 12. The lower half is 3, 5, 8, 10 and its median is (5 + 8) ÷ 2 = 6.5." } ``` ### Box length ### Upper fence ### Review ## Make: how late is a normal day? ```step stage: make insight: "Back to Route 1: decide whether the 15-minute day is an outlier and say how late a normal day is." tasks: - hint: ["Quartiles first: lower five 0, 1, 2, 2, 3 and upper five 4, 5, 6, 8, 15.", "Q3 + 1.5 × IQR."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "Route 1's 11 lateness values are 0, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 8 and 15 minutes. Find the upper fence and decide whether 15 is an outlier." steps: - ["median $= 4$; lower half $0, 1, 2, 2, 3$ gives $Q_1 = 2$; upper half $4, 5, 6, 8, 15$ gives $Q_3 = 6$", "the quartiles"] - ["$6 - 2 = 4$", "the interquartile range"] - ["$6 + 1.5 \\times 4 = 12$", "the upper fence"] - ["$15 > 12$, so 15 is an outlier", "beyond the fence"] answer: "12" answerLabel: "Upper fence (minutes)" tolerance: 0.01 feedback: - ["10", "That is the upper quartile plus the IQR. The rule uses 1.5 times the IQR."] - ["15", "That is the highest value. The fence is the upper quartile plus 1.5 times the IQR."] criteria: - "I found both quartiles." - "I used 1.5 times the interquartile range." - "I compared 15 with the fence and said what it means." explain: "The quartiles are 2 and 6, the IQR is 4, and the upper fence is 6 + 1.5 × 4 = 12. The 15-minute day is beyond it, so it's an outlier: a one-off bad day, not what the bus is usually like." - check: type: question q: "What is the best description of a normal day on Route 1?" options: - "Between about 2 and 6 minutes late, with the middle at 4 minutes" - "15 minutes late" - "Between 0 and 15 minutes late, with the middle at 7.5" - "On time" answer: 0 feedback: - null - "That was the one outlier." - "That is the whole range, including the outlier, and 7.5 is the middle of the range, not the median." - "Only the first day was on time." explain: "The box is the middle half of the days, 2 to 6 minutes late, and the median is 4. The 15 is a one-off." ``` ### The outlier Work this out on paper first, then type your answer. ### A normal day The bus and its days are made up for the task. **Also used in** - **Waiting times.** Hospitals, call centres and train operators report how long people wait with boxes and medians. - **Sport.** Race times and scores for a season are often shown as boxplots. - **Next lesson.** Comparing with boxplots: two routes, side by side. ```teacher summary: "Students draw and read a boxplot from the five numbers: the box is the middle half, the bar is the median, the whiskers reach the furthest values inside the 1.5 × IQR fences, and values beyond them are outliers (AC9M10ST02, node 2)." time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 14 min · Modify 10 min · Practise and Make 13 min goals: - I can say what each part of a boxplot shows. - I can find the fences and say whether a value is an outlier. - I can read how late a normal day is from the box. struggle: "Reading the box as how many values there are, or the whiskers as the box. Ask: what fraction of the days is inside the box, whatever its length?" before: > Students need the five numbers from the previous lesson. This is a hinge lesson: students who misread the median bar or read box width as how many values there are can't compare distributions in the next lesson. The board draws a boxplot with the median-of-halves quartiles from the previous lesson. With `outliers: on` the whiskers stop at the last value inside the fences (upper quartile + 1.5 × IQR and lower quartile − 1.5 × IQR) and a cross marks each outlier; a value exactly on a fence is not an outlier. The 1.5 rule is a convention that the lesson states, not something students derive; it is a fine moment to say that other rules exist. The bus, its minutes late and the second route are made up for the task. The library entry (bus-lateness) suggests the class records two real routes for a few weeks and checks the comparison holds; that is a good real-data follow-up. running: - "Predict: show of hands before the check. Hold the picture up and ask where half the days sit." - "Run: ask which number will change before anyone edits the 15." - "Paper: the fence try-one and the Make are worked on paper first." - "Modify: all-the-same and the value on the fence are the edge cases." stuck: - see: A student says the box is where most of the values are, so a wider box has more values. ask: How many of the 11 days are inside the box, and would that change if the box were wider? fix: About half of the days are in the box whatever its width. A wider box means the middle half is more spread out. - see: A student draws the whisker to the outlier. ask: Is that value beyond the fence? fix: If it is, mark it with a cross and stop the whisker at the highest value inside the fence. - see: A student uses 1.5 × the median for the fence. ask: What does the fence measure from, and what is it a multiple of? fix: It measures from the box's end, a distance of 1.5 times the IQR. stretch: Make up five values that give an IQR of zero but a range of 10. Draw the boxplot. support: Mark the five numbers on a number line on paper first, draw the box between the quartiles, then add the median bar and whiskers. leads: > Continues AC9M10ST02 (node 2; a hinge). Where it leads: comparing distributions with boxplots (next), where two routes sit one above the other. exit: q: A boxplot's five numbers are 5, 8, 12, 20 and 41. What is the upper fence, and is 41 an outlier? a: IQR = 12; fence = 20 + 18 = 38; 41 is beyond it, so it's an outlier. explain: > A boxplot draws the five numbers as a picture. The box runs from the lower quartile to the upper quartile, the bar inside is the median, and the whiskers reach the lowest and highest values that aren't outliers. A value is an outlier if it is more than 1.5 times the interquartile range beyond the box. It is marked with a cross. ```

# Boards for "Boxplots". Route 1's lateness on 11 school days, in minutes (made up). The Values box changes the data.

# region: run
widget: data
values: 0, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 8, 15
range: 0, 20
step: 1

view: box

outliers: on
label: Minutes late

# Dev's working for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: dev
Route 1's box runs from 2 to 6 minutes late.
Route 2's box runs from 4 to 6 minutes late, so it is narrower.
A narrower box means fewer buses ran on Route 2.
So Route 1 is the busier route.
